templates.scenario: At a team meeting at {workplace|the}, your {lead} asks for ideas to shorten how long {client.plural} wait for service. You are new, and a few coworkers have already shared ideas. You have a thought, but you are not sure it would work perfectly.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Share your idea, explain how it would work, and ask the team what problems they see in it.
options.why: Offering an idea with a clear explanation gives the team something to build on, and inviting feedback improves it. Ideas do not have to be perfect to be useful.

options.text: Keep it to yourself until you are certain it would work perfectly in every situation.
options.why: Few ideas are flawless at first. Teams improve ideas together, so holding one back means the group never gets the chance to refine it.
options.misconception: An idea is only worth sharing if it is flawless.

options.text: Wait to see which idea your {lead} likes best and then agree with that one.
options.why: Agreeing with the leading idea adds nothing new. Your fresh view as a newer employee may notice things others stopped seeing.
options.misconception: Backing the popular idea is safer than offering my own.

options.text: Tell the group you are too new to have useful ideas about how things are done around here yet.
options.why: Newer employees often spot problems experienced staff no longer notice. Being new is a reason to share what you see, not to stay quiet.
options.misconception: New employees have nothing to add.

templates.principle: Contribute ideas openly, explain them clearly, and welcome feedback; a rough idea can become a good one once a team works on it.

review.notes: Beginner; a supportive meeting is implied by the lead asking for ideas. No policy or legal content.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. While doing {task|the}, you notice a step that your team repeats every day and that adds about ten minutes without improving the result. You have an idea for a simpler way. Changing {task|the} is up to your {lead}.

options.text: Describe the extra step and your simpler idea to your {lead}, with an example of the time it costs.
options.why: A specific proposal with evidence gives the person who owns the procedure what they need to decide. It improves the process without surprising your teammates.

options.text: Start using your simpler method tomorrow without telling anyone, and see whether results improve.
options.why: Changing a shared procedure on your own can create confusion or errors for teammates who expect the usual steps. The owner should decide.
options.misconception: It is easier to ask forgiveness than permission.

options.text: Tell coworkers how pointless the step is, and hope the comment eventually reaches someone who is able to change it.
options.why: Venting spreads frustration but does not put a proposal in front of the decision-maker. An idea only improves the process if it is presented.
options.misconception: Complaining informally is the same as proposing a change.

options.text: Wait for the next scheduled improvement project, since fixing processes is not your job.
options.why: Useful ideas can come from anyone doing the work. Waiting keeps a known time-waster in place when a simple idea is ready now.
options.misconception: Improvement ideas should only come from assigned projects.

templates.principle: Bring improvement ideas to the person who owns the process, with a specific example, instead of changing things quietly or only complaining.

review.notes: Lead ownership of the procedure is stated.

templates.timing: The proposal is the first step; changing or complaining skips the decision-maker.

templates.scenario: Your team at {workplace|a} wants to improve how a routine job gets done.
templates.prompt: Arrange these improvement steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Identify what is slowing the job down
Try the most promising change on a small scale
Review the results and adjust before adopting the change

precedence.why: Ideas aim better when you know exactly what the problem is.
You need options before you can pick the most promising one to test.
You can only judge a change after you have seen how it works in practice.

templates.principle: Improve a process step by step: define the problem, generate options, test small, then review before adopting.

review.notes: A natural chain; every step depends on the previous one.

templates.scenario: Your {lead} asks you to improve the quality of {deliverable|the} for an important day at {workplace|the}, with no extra budget. In a storage room you find unused materials that might help. No one has said whether they are available for use.

options.text: Look at what is available, sketch a low-cost plan using those materials, and check with your {lead} before using them.
options.why: Starting from what you already have meets the no-budget limit creatively, and checking first respects that someone else may own those materials.

options.text: Ask your {lead} for a small budget so you can buy new materials that are designed for this exact job.
options.why: Asking is reasonable, but it skips the creative challenge of using what is already on hand, which is what the limit was meant to encourage.

options.text: Use the stored materials right away since no one is using them, and explain later if asked.
options.why: Unused does not mean free to take. Materials may be reserved for something else, so permission comes before use.
options.misconception: Anything sitting unused is available to anyone.

options.text: Tell your {lead} that nothing can be improved without more money, and carry on as usual.
options.why: Limited resources are a reason to be inventive, not a reason to stop. A plan using materials on hand was available.
options.misconception: A limited budget makes improvement impossible.

templates.principle: With limited resources, start with what you already have, plan a low-cost option, and confirm you may use shared materials before using them.

review.notes: Acceptable option is reasonable but skips the resourceful approach; no legal claims.

templates.scenario: A team at {workplace|the} shares these notes after a brainstorming session.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that shuts down creativity.

segments.text: We brainstormed ways to shorten customer wait times.
segments.whyFine: A clear statement of the session's purpose.

segments.text: One idea was sending text-message reminders.
Another idea was rearranging the waiting area.
I said none of these would work because we have never tried anything like them.
segments.why: Rejecting ideas only because they are new shuts down creativity and skips the chance to test whether they work.

segments.text: We will pick one idea to test next week.
segments.whyFine: Planning a test is a constructive way to move forward.

templates.principle: Judge ideas on their merits and test them; being new is not a reason to dismiss an idea.

review.notes: Single line dismisses ideas for being untried.
